Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

Musical artist

**McKinley Morganfield** (April 4, 1913 – April 30, 1983),[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGordon20024–5-2) better known as **Muddy Waters**, was an American [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") singer-songwriter and musician who was an important figure in the post-World War II blues scene, and is often cited as the "father of modern [Chicago blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_blues "Chicago blues")".[[3]](#cite_note-cantbe-dvd-3)

Muddy Waters grew up on [Stovall Plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stovall,_Mississippi "Stovall, Mississippi") near [Clarksdale, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarksdale,_Mississippi "Clarksdale, Mississippi"), and by the age of 17 was playing the guitar and the harmonica, copying local blues artists [Son House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Son_House "Son House") and [Robert Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Johnson "Robert Johnson").[[4]](#cite_note-Guralnick-4) In 1941, [Alan Lomax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Lomax "Alan Lomax") and professor [John W. Work III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_W._Work_III "John W. Work III") of [Fisk University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_University "Fisk University") recorded him in Mississippi for the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress").[[5]](#cite_note-Palmer-5)[[6]](#cite_note-PBS-6) In 1943, he moved to Chicago to become a full-time professional musician. In 1946, he recorded his first records for [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") and then for [Aristocrat Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocrat_Records "Aristocrat Records"), a newly formed label run by brothers [Leonard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Chess "Leonard Chess") and [Phil Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Chess "Phil Chess").

In the early 1950s, Muddy Waters and his band—[Little Walter Jacobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Walter_Jacobs "Little Walter Jacobs") on harmonica, [Jimmy Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Rogers "Jimmy Rogers") on guitar, [Elga Edmonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elga_Edmonds "Elga Edmonds") (also known as Elgin Evans) on drums and [Otis Spann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis_Spann "Otis Spann") on piano—recorded several songs that became blues classics, some with the bassist and songwriter [Willie Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Dixon "Willie Dixon"). These songs included "[Hoochie Coochie Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoochie_Coochie_Man "Hoochie Coochie Man")", "[I Just Want to Make Love to You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Just_Want_to_Make_Love_to_You "I Just Want to Make Love to You")" and "[I'm Ready](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Ready_(Muddy_Waters_song) "I'm Ready (Muddy Waters song)")". In 1958, he traveled to England, laying the foundations of the resurgence of interest in the blues there. His performance at the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival") in 1960 was recorded and released as his first live album, *[At Newport 1960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_Newport_1960 "At Newport 1960")*.

Muddy Waters' music laid the foundation for various [American music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_the_United_States "Music of the United States") genres, including [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") and subsequently rock.

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Muddy_Waters&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Muddy Waters' place and date of birth are not conclusively known. He stated that he was born in 1915 at [Rolling Fork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Fork,_Mississippi "Rolling Fork, Mississippi") in [Sharkey County, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharkey_County,_Mississippi "Sharkey County, Mississippi"), but other evidence suggests that he was born in the unincorporated community of Jug's Corner, in neighboring [Issaquena County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issaquena_County,_Mississippi "Issaquena County, Mississippi"), in 1913.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGordon20023-7) In the 1930s and 1940s, before his rise to fame, the year of his birth was reported as 1913 on his marriage license, recording notes, and musicians' union card. A 1955 interview in the *[Chicago Defender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Defender "Chicago Defender")* is the earliest in which he stated 1915 as the year of his birth, and he continued to state that year in interviews from that point onward. The 1920 census lists him as five years old as of March 6, 1920. The Social Security Death Index, relying on the [Social Security card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_card "Social Security card") application submitted after his move to Chicago in the mid-1940s, lists him as being born April 4, 1913. His gravestone gives his birth year as 1915.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

His grandmother, Della Grant, raised him after his mother died shortly after his birth. Grant gave him the nickname "Muddy" at an early age because he loved to play in the muddy water of nearby [Deer Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deer_Creek_(Mississippi) "Deer Creek (Mississippi)").[[9]](#cite_note-9) "Waters" was added years later, as he began to play harmonica and perform locally in his early teens.[[10]](#cite_note-10) He taught himself to play harmonica.[[11]](#cite_note-11) The remains of the cabin on Stovall Plantation where he lived in his youth are now at the [Delta Blues Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Blues_Museum "Delta Blues Museum") in [Clarksdale, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarksdale,_Mississippi "Clarksdale, Mississippi").[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)

He had his first introduction to music in church: "I used to belong to church. I was a good Baptist, singing in the church. So I got all of my good moaning and trembling going on for me right out of church," he recalled. By the time he was 17, he had purchased his first guitar. "I sold the last horse that we had. Made about fifteen dollars for him, gave my grandmother seven dollars and fifty cents, I kept seven-fifty and paid about two-fifty for that guitar. It was a [Stella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stella_(guitar) "Stella (guitar)"). The people ordered them from [Sears-Roebuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears-Roebuck "Sears-Roebuck") in Chicago."[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESzatmary20148-14) He started playing his songs in joints near his hometown, mostly on a plantation owned by Colonel [William Howard Stovall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Howard_Stovall "William Howard Stovall").[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPalmer19824-15)

"He brought his stuff down and recorded me right in my house," Muddy told *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* magazine, "and when he played back the first song I sounded just like anybody's records. **Waters** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2012, after the American musician McKinley Morganfield, better known as [Muddy Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muddy_Waters "Muddy Waters").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The crater has a bright [ray system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_system "Ray system"), as well as an unusual dark flow-feature associated with the southern rim. The flow-feature is interpreted as [impact melt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_melt "Impact melt").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

**Armstrong** is a small, bowl-shaped lunar [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") located in the southern part of the [Mare Tranquillitatis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare_Tranquillitatis "Mare Tranquillitatis").[[2]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-2) It lies about 50 kilometers to the northeast of the [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11") landing site, [Tranquility Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tranquility_Base "Tranquility Base"). Named after American astronaut [Neil Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Armstrong "Neil Armstrong") (1930-2012),[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1) the crater is the easternmost of the row of three craters named in honor of the Apollo 11 crew members. Their designations were formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970. To the north is the [Ranger 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranger_8 "Ranger 8") impact site.[[3]](#cite_note-Chu_et_al_2012-3)

This crater was previously identified as **Sabine E**[[4]](#cite_note-Moore_Rees_2014-4) before being renamed by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970.[[5]](#cite_note-McElheny_1970-5) [Sabine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabine_(crater) "Sabine (crater)") itself is located due west of Armstrong.[[2]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-2)

**Joplin** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2012, after the American composer [Scott Joplin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Joplin "Scott Joplin").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Joplin's [peak ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") is relatively small compared to the crater diameter and it is offset from the center. It is one of 110 peak ring basins on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Joplin is located about half-way between the prominent crater [Debussy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debussy_(crater) "Debussy (crater)") and the crater [Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lennon_(crater) "Lennon (crater)"). It is south of the crater [Travers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travers_(crater) "Travers (crater)"). Together with crater [Bulsara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulsara_(crater) "Bulsara (crater)") (named after [Freddie Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury "Freddie Mercury")), Lennon and Joplin form a line of nearly equally spaced craters.[[3]](#cite_note-3)
